t: Zengi's capture of the County of Edessa after the siege of 1144 made him a hero in the Muslim world; he was assassinated by a slave two years later.
Nur ad-Din took Damascus from the Burids in 1154 and, through his general Shirkuh and Shirkuh's nephew Saladin, brought Fatimid Egypt under Zengid dominion in 1169.
Saladin crushed the armies of Mosul and Aleppo at the Horns of Hama on 13 April 1175 and received Aleppo on 12 June 1183, ending Zengid rule in Syria.
dyk: When Saladin took Amid from the Zengid coalition in April 1183, the Ayyubids counted among its stores 80,000 candles, a tower full of arrowheads and 1,040,000 books.
ev: After the murder of Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi, the Seljuk Empire names Zengi, son of Aq Sunqur al-Hajib, atabeg of Mosul.
Zengi captures the County of Edessa from the Crusaders after the siege of Edessa, a feat that makes him a hero in the Muslim world.
Nur ad-Din captures Damascus from the Turkic Burid dynasty and rules Syria from there.
Shirkuh kills the vizier Shawar and seizes Egypt as Fatimid vizier in Nur ad-Din's name; on his death the same year his nephew Saladin succeeds him.
Nur ad-Din dies on 15 May; his eleven-year-old son as-Salih Ismail inherits, and Saladin enters Damascus on 23 November.
Imad ad-Din Zangi hands Aleppo to Saladin on 12 June in exchange for Sinjar, Nusaybin and Raqqa, ending Zengid rule in Syria.
Badr al-Din Lu'lu', atabeg to the child emirs of Mosul, takes the city in his own name, possibly after murdering the last Zengid emir Nasir ad-Din Mahmud.
Al-Jazira in northern Iraq, the last Zengid territory, falls to an-Nasir Yusuf, the Ayyubid emir of Aleppo.

f.capital: Mosul; Aleppo from 1128; Damascus from 1154 under Nur ad-Din
f.founder: Imad al-Din Zengi, appointed Seljuk atabeg of Mosul in 1127
f.predecessor: The Seljuk atabegate of Mosul under Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi; the Artuqids in Aleppo and the Burid dynasty in Damascus
f.successor: The Ayyubids under Saladin (Damascus 1174, Aleppo 1183, al-Jazira 1250); Badr al-Din Lu'lu' in Mosul from 1234
